1. Introduction: The “Bracket Tax” on Your AI Budget
In the world of AI infrastructure, we’ve spent years optimizing our models, but we’re still sending data in a delivery vehicle that’s bleeding us dry. If you’re building production LLM apps and still using JSON as your primary input format, you are paying a literal “bracket tax.”
Every double quote, curly brace, and comma in your JSON payload is processed as a token. In an economy where you are billed per token – and where context windows have a “high-accuracy sweet spot” – sending redundant structural syntax is a form of technical debt that costs real money. I’ll admit, I was skeptical when I first saw TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation). Another “better” data format? But after digging into the benchmarks, it’s clear: we’ve been optimizing the wrong side of the equation.
2. Takeaway 1: JSON is “Noisy” for AI Models
The core problem is that JSON was designed for human readability and web standards, not for the way an LLM’s neural network processes information. For a model, JSON is incredibly “noisy.” It forces the LLM to parse tons of structural syntax – the repeated keys in an array of objects are particularly egregious – before it even gets to the actual data.
As noted by the team at Better Stack:
When you scale this up – logs, metrics, chat histories – the token cost skyrockets, and that’s what we’re paying for if we’re using JSON still, because all of these are just tokens to an LLM.”
We’ve stuck with JSON because the ecosystem is massive and the tooling is familiar. But for an AI infrastructure engineer, those brackets are just filler. LLMs don’t need the constant reminder of what a key is called for every single entry in a list. They are remarkably good at understanding structure with much less hand-holding.
3. Takeaway 2: The 60% Token Reduction is Real
The efficiency gains of TOON aren’t just theoretical. In benchmarks involving large-scale logs, TOON demonstrated a massive reduction in payload size. Specifically, a log dataset that cost 1,236 tokens in JSON was compressed to just 454 tokens using TOON – a 63% reduction.
TOON achieves this by using a header-first tabular format for arrays and YAML-like indentation to signify structure. Instead of repeating keys for every row, it defines the structure once at the top and provides the data immediately after. It’s the compactness of a CSV with the explicit structure an LLM needs to remain reliable.

4. Takeaway 3: Accuracy vs. Format (The Surprise Winner)
There’s a counter-intuitive “Accuracy Paradox” in LLM data processing: compacted JSON is often more accurate than “pretty” JSON. While we find whitespace and tabs helpful, they often distract or “confuse” the model. TOON leans into this by stripping the noise, which can actually increase retrieval accuracy by roughly 4%.
More importantly, token reduction isn’t just about cost – it’s about model reliability. Benchmarks show that models like Gemini 1.5 Flash and GPT-4o Nano are the current champions at retrieving data from “giant piles of bullshit” (as Theo – t3.gg puts it). In contrast, models like Claude or Groq show a significant decline in accuracy once queries exceed the first 1,000 tokens. By using TOON, you keep your data within that high-accuracy “sweet spot” of the model’s context window.
5. Takeaway 4: The “Nested” Weakness – When to Stick with JSON
TOON isn’t a silver bullet for every data structure. Benchmarks are generally split into two categories:
The Flat Only Track: Uniform arrays (logs, product catalogs, metrics). This is where TOON “crushes” JSON.
The Mixed Structure Track: Heavily nested or non-uniform data.
Pro-Tip: If your data is a uniform list of 500 server logs, use TOON. If your data is a deeply nested, irregular tree of recursive logic, stick to compacted JSON. TOON tends to get “confused” when it loses the tabular advantage of uniform keys.
6. Takeaway 5: TOON as a Translation Layer, Not a Language Replacement
The beauty of TOON is that it doesn’t require you to rewrite your codebase. You should still use JSON programmatically within your application. TOON acts as a translation layer at the edge. Right before you hit the API, you call an encode() function.
Implementation is dead simple via the @tune-format/tune package:
NPM Package: Use encode(myJsonObject) to transform your data before the fetch.
CLI Tool: For those of us in the trenches, there is a TOON CLI. You can dump data with bash scripts locally and pipe it directly into a token-optimized format for testing.
Even the most skeptical “vibe coders” are coming around. As Theo – t3.gg noted during a live deep-dive:
“This is weirdly thought out and actually useful… I see genuine value in this. If you are actually passing JSON arrays to your models, you really should go give this a shot.”
7. Conclusion: The Future of Token-Aware Development
We are moving away from data formats optimized for humans and toward formats optimized for machine context. “Token-aware” development is the next logical step in AI infrastructure. By moving from raw JSON to TOON, you aren’t just saving money – you’re increasing the reliability of your model’s output by giving it less “noise” to filter through.
If you could improve your retrieval accuracy and cut your API bill in half with a single call, why are you still paying the bracket tax?
